solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Food which uses spinach in a way

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: a lane is a narrow road or path
sag or saag is the Indian word for spinach, as in sag aloo

explanation.surface: A cook describing a dish that works spinach in by some method.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a way' reads as 'after a fashion', but it is the container instruction plus the thing that holds. Spinach is the Indian-menu word, familiar from curry houses.
explanation.definitionFit: Lasagne is a baked Italian pasta dish, layered sheets with sauce, so it is an example of a meal.

clue.text: Healthy and vigorous education?

blocks.note: lite food is the low-fat, healthy version
racy can mean lively and spirited

explanation.surface: A school prospectus promising pupils a healthy and energetic time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Healthy and vigorous' reads as one description of a lifestyle, but each adjective gives half. The question mark admits the definition is an example rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Reading and writing ability is the core outcome of schooling, so the setter offers it as an example, flagged with a query.

clue.text: Thin girl’s bottom shown in poster

indicators.note: in a down entry the bottom of a word is its final letter
something shown in a frame sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: one who posts a letter is a poster, or sender

explanation.surface: A gossip column noticing a skinny model's behind on a billboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poster' is a billboard in the surface, but here it is a person who posts things: a SENDER.
explanation.definitionFit: Slender and thin are straightforward synonyms describing a slight, narrow build or figure.

clue.text: With distortion one’s stereo might fall apart

indicators.note: distorting something bends it out of its proper shape, so the letters lose their order

explanation.surface: Crank the volume until the sound distorts and your hi-fi might break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Distortion' is audio jargon in the surface, making it a camouflaged anagram indicator; the fifteen letters of 'one's stereo might' are the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To go to smithereens is an idiom for shattering into tiny fragments, collapsing completely into pieces.

clue.text: Shade found in English vineyard

blocks.note: a cru is a French wine-growing estate or its classified growth

explanation.surface: A particular colour spotted at a wine estate in England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found in' tempts a hidden-word hunt through 'English vineyard', but nothing fits; it just joins the shade to the wordplay E plus CRU.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecru is a pale greyish-yellow colour, like unbleached linen, so it is one particular hue.

clue.text: Takes away help to stop crossing channel

indicators.note: to cross something here is to span it end to end, so one piece straddles the other

blocks.note: ABS is the anti-lock braking system, a car's aid to stopping
a duct is a pipe or channel

explanation.surface: Coastguards withdrawing a rescue service meant to halt Channel crossings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Channel' looks like the English Channel and 'help to stop' like a halt to crossings; in fact the help is a car's anti-lock brakes, known by their initials.
explanation.definitionFit: To abduct someone is to carry them off by force, a kidnapping sense of removal.

clue.text: See prize rise in value

blocks.note: to see and to prize are both senses of recognising and valuing something
said of property or shares that grow more valuable

explanation.surface: An auctioneer watching a trophy's price climb.
explanation.walkthrough: In fact there are three definitions: 'See' (understand), 'prize' (treasure) and 'rise in value' each give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Appreciating means both grasping or valuing something highly and, of assets, gaining monetary worth over time.

clue.text: How to make edge of screen?

definitions.text: How to make edge of screen?

blocks.note: the surface: the border of a monitor or cinema screen
the setter's reading: a screen can be a hedge, and a speaker who leaves off the opening H turns that into an edge

explanation.surface: A technical question about manufacturing the rim of a display.
explanation.walkthrough: A hedge is a screen of shrubs; say it with a Cockney accent, losing the H sound, and it becomes 'edge'. AITCH is how the letter H is spelt out.
explanation.definitionFit: Omitting the H sound at the start of words is a stereotyped feature of Cockney and other working-class English accents.

clue.text: Film maker‘s place in company

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: the abbreviation used in street addresses
a chain is a company with many branches

explanation.surface: A director landing a job at a studio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Company' wants to be CO, the usual abbreviation, but here it is a group of shops trading under one name.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlie Chaplin wrote, directed and starred in silent comedies such as The Kid and Modern Times.

clue.text: Hot clothes not right in dirty accommodation

indicators.note: 'not' removes something, and the thing removed is the abbreviation for right
one thing sitting in another is enclosed by it

explanation.surface: Warm garments stuffed into a grubby flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot' is the definition in its sense of perspiring, not of fashionable or stolen.
explanation.definitionFit: Being hot makes you perspire, so a warm, clammy person is described with the word for perspiring.

clue.text: Lifting not just any old foot

blocks.note: said emphatically, 'the' means the one and only, not just any
the abbreviation of the foot, an old imperial measure

explanation.surface: A physio insisting on raising one specific leg, not any old one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifting' looks like raising a foot, but it is slang for stealing, as in shoplifting.
explanation.definitionFit: Lifting is informal for stealing, so the act of taking goods without paying is its noun equivalent.

clue.text: Soldiers will copy someone depraved

blocks.note: probate is the official proving of a will, and the certified copy issued with it

explanation.surface: Army recruits who will imitate a bad example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will' is a legal document, not the future tense, and 'will copy' is one idea: PROBATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A reprobate is an unprincipled rogue, a person of immoral, corrupt character.

clue.text: It’s usually hot or fairly cool?

blocks.note: rad is slang for cool or excellent

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about something that is either warm or chilly.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in reverse clue order: 'fairly cool' means cool-ish, with the slang word first. 'Hot' means peppery, not warm.
explanation.definitionFit: Radishes are peppery root vegetables, so their taste is typically sharp and pungent, hot in flavour terms.

clue.text: A film about hilarious old company in 18

indicators.note: to go about something is to go round it, so one piece surrounds others

blocks.note: internet shorthand for rolling on the floor laughing

explanation.surface: A documentary about a comic firm of years gone by in Russia.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 refers to the answer at 18-down, RUSSIA. 'Hilarious' is not an anagram indicator; it is internet slang for laughing hard.
explanation.definitionFit: Aeroflot is the Russian national airline, a Soviet-era carrier still flying from Moscow.

clue.text: Traveller from literature toddler gets excited about

indicators.note: an excited child is all over the place, so the letters are stirred up
to go about something is to go round it, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: the standard short form, as in English Lit

explanation.surface: A small child getting worked up over a character from a storybook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Traveller from literature' reads as the whole definition, but 'literature' is wordplay, held inside the shuffled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Hugh Lofting's doctor who talks to animals voyages widely in the books, notably to Spidermonkey Island.

clue.text: Bird‘s rotting flesh cut by beast feeding before

indicators.note: something cut by a blade has that blade driven into its middle
food being fed goes inside, so one piece is put into another

explanation.surface: A vulture's carcass torn into by an animal that was eating first.
explanation.walkthrough: Two containers nest: the beast feeds into the old word for before, and that whole piece cuts the rotting flesh.
explanation.definitionFit: A carrier pigeon is a homing pigeon trained to fly messages back to its loft.

clue.text: Dry fruit all over flower

indicators.note: in a down entry, going over turns a word upside down, so it reads backwards

explanation.surface: Dried fruit scattered across a flower bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All over' reads as everywhere, but it is ALL flipped.
explanation.definitionFit: Prunella, or self-heal, is a low-growing plant of the mint family with purple blooms.

clue.text: Chocolates chewed by the woman who has class?

indicators.note: chewed food is mashed up, so the letters are mangled

explanation.surface: A classy lady nibbling a box of chocolates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Class' in the surface means refinement; in the answer it is a room of pupils.
explanation.definitionFit: A teacher takes charge of a group of pupils, so the one with a form group is an educator.

clue.text: Dog that is rejected after biting

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so it turns round

blocks.note: a biting wind or remark is sharp

explanation.surface: A pet turned away from the shelter after it bit someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay order is reversed: 'after biting' puts SHARP first.
explanation.definitionFit: The shar-pei is a Chinese breed known for deep folds of wrinkled skin.

clue.text: Buoy made of clay’s hard on top

indicators.note: in a down entry the top is the start, so a letter is moved to the front

blocks.note: earthen pots are made of baked clay

explanation.surface: A float made of pottery that is tough on its upper side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buoy' is a verb here, to cheer up. The H in EARTHEN moves to the top of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: To buoy someone up is to lift their spirits, which is to encourage or cheer them.

clue.text: A leather article is certainly short from the bottom

definitions.note: the answer is a kind of leather, a noun used attributively

indicators.note: cutting something short trims its final letter
in a down entry, reading from the bottom goes upwards, backwards

explanation.surface: A leather goods label that is definitely cut short at the bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: A, IS and SUR are read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Russia leather is a durable birch-oil-tanned hide once used for bookbinding, so the country names a type.

clue.text: Confident United about to intensify attack

blocks.note: UN is the United Nations, trimmed to its first word
f, forte, the musical direction to play loudly

explanation.surface: A football report: a self-assured United side is about to step up its attack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'United' is a football team in the surface; here it is UN.
explanation.definitionFit: Being without fear means feeling bold and self-assured, a close synonym for confident.

clue.text: Son’s direct descendants

blocks.note: to train a hose or gun is to aim, direct it

explanation.surface: A family tree tracing a son's direct line of heirs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Direct' is an adjective in the surface, but a verb in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A strain is a line of descent, a lineage or breed of offspring from common ancestors.

clue.text: Jeremy Thorpe’s inner fantasy

indicators.note: the inner part of a phrase is found within it, so the letters lie inside

blocks.note: spans the end of the first name and the start of the surname

explanation.surface: The private dream life of Jeremy Thorpe, the scandal-hit Liberal leader.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeremy Thorpe led the British Liberal Party in the 1960s and 70s.
explanation.definitionFit: A myth is a made-up story or false belief, something imagined rather than real.

clue.text: With wisdom, plan is yet to develop

indicators.note: developing means changing form, so the letters take a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A cautious sage: the scheme still has some way to go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' looks like a link word, but it belongs to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Sapient means wise, from Latin sapere, so its adverb describes acting sagely.

clue.text: Follower of golf starts to hear of the easy life

indicators.note: the start of each word is its opening letter, so only those are kept

blocks.note: the initials of the five words

explanation.surface: A lazy golfer's dream of leisure on the course.
explanation.walkthrough: In the NATO phonetic alphabet, Golf is G and the next word, for H, is Hotel.
explanation.definitionFit: Radio operators spell G then H as Golf then Hotel, so the second codeword comes directly after the first.

clue.text: A biological matter being discussed

blocks.note: tissue is organic material, cells of a plant or animal

explanation.surface: A science seminar with a biology topic on the agenda.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Matter' looks like a topic here, but it is physical stuff.
explanation.definitionFit: A point at issue is the one under debate, the question currently in dispute.

clue.text: Praise Ford Scorpio, extremely hard to reverse

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only those letters are kept
reversing runs backwards, so the order is turned round

blocks.note: Anna Ford, a BBC and ITN newsreader

explanation.surface: A car review praising a Ford Scorpio that is very difficult to back up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ford Scorpio' is a real car, but it splits: Ford is Anna Ford, a British TV newsreader, and Scorpio gives its outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Hosanna is a shout of adoration to God, used in hymns and liturgy as an exclamation of worship.
